title: Queue Journey
description: Queue and deque design, streaming candidates, BFS layers, dependencies, and shortest paths.

journey.outcome: Recognize when arrival order, candidate expiry, or a breadth-first frontier calls for a queue.

connections.implement-queue-using-array: Begin with FIFO: the oldest remaining item leaves first. Separate the positions used for reading and writing instead of shifting the array on every removal.
connections.implement-queue-using-linked-list: Keep the same FIFO contract while changing the storage. Front and rear node references replace array indices; notice what must happen when the last item leaves.
connections.design-circular-queue: Return to array storage and reuse freed positions. A circular buffer separates logical order from physical indices and makes empty-versus-full state an explicit design decision.
connections.design-circular-deque: Extend the circular queue to both ends without changing its storage model. Front insertion and rear deletion introduce backward wraparound and more boundary cases.
connections.queue-reversal: Now deliberately change arrival order. A stack reverses items taken from a queue, connecting the two data structures through their opposite removal rules.
connections.reverse-first-k-elements-of-queue: Refine full reversal into a prefix operation. Reverse only the first k items, then rotate the untouched suffix so it remains behind the reversed prefix.
connections.interleave-queue-halves: Instead of reversing a prefix, weave two arrival-ordered streams together. Keep track of which half owns each item and preserve the order within each half.
connections.implement-queue-using-stacks: Turn the reversal idea into an implementation technique. Two stacks can restore FIFO order, and postponing transfers until necessary makes operations amortized O(1).
connections.implement-stack-using-queues: Reverse the previous emulation: expose LIFO using FIFO operations. Rotating existing items behind a new arrival places the newest value at the front.
connections.generate-binary-numbers: Use the queue as a frontier of unfinished work. Removing one binary string and appending its two children produces values in breadth-first order.
connections.first-non-repeating-in-a-stream: Keep arrival order, but discard candidates that stop being valid. A frequency table tells you whether the oldest candidate can still answer the next stream query.
connections.first-negative-in-every-window: A candidate can now expire because it is too old, not because it repeats. Store indices so the front can be removed as the fixed-size window advances.
connections.sliding-window-maximum: Extend the previous window queue into a deque. Remove expired indices from the front and candidates dominated by a newer, larger value from the back.
connections.design-minmax-queue: Turn the sliding-window maximum into a reusable queue API. Keep ordinary FIFO storage plus increasing and decreasing candidate deques, preserving duplicate minima and maxima.
connections.binary-tree-level-order-traversal: Return to the frontier from binary-number generation, this time with tree nodes. Snapshot the current queue size to separate one level from the children it creates.
connections.rotting-oranges: Generalize level-order traversal to a grid with many starting nodes. One queue seeded with every rotten orange models simultaneous spreading; each BFS layer is one minute.
connections.course-schedule: A frontier can mean ready work rather than physical distance. Queue courses with no remaining prerequisites and release their dependents; unprocessed courses expose a dependency cycle.
connections.course-schedule-ii: Reuse the same indegree-removal process and retain the processing order. A valid schedule must include every course, including independent courses in disconnected components.
connections.word-ladder: Return to distance layers, now in an implicit graph of words. Generate valid one-letter neighbors as needed, and mark them visited when queued so the first arrival is the shortest transformation.
